UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                       )
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                        )                Docket No. ER26-3380-000
                                                       )


                   ANSWER AND MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER
                  OF THE INDEPENDENT MARKET MONITOR FOR PJM

          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules and Regulations, 1

Monitoring Analytics, LLC, acting in its capacity as the Independent Market Monitor

(“Market Monitor”) for PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”), 2 submits this answer to, and

moves for leave to answer, the answer submitted by PJM on September 10, 2026 (“September

10th Answer”).

          The proceeding concerns the filing submitted by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”)

on July 31, 2026, proposing (at 1) “to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement

(“RBP”)—a one-time procurement of new capacity to address resource adequacy challenges

in the PJM Region arising from insufficient commitments of capacity in the 2027/2028 and

2028/2029 Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) Auctions, primarily driven by the

unprecedented addition of large loads, most notably data centers” (“RBP Filing”).

          Despite the clearly stated public policy goals of elected officials, PJM’s stated purpose

is not to assign the costs and risks of data centers to data centers. PJM’s stated purpose is not

to protect other PJM customers from paying the costs and bearing the risks caused by data




1       18 CFR §§ 385.212 & 385.213 (2025).

2       Capitalized terms used herein and not otherwise defined have the meaning used in the PJM Open
        Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”), the PJM Operating Agreement (“OA”) or the PJM Reliability
        Assurance Agreement (“RAA”).
 centers. The shortfall identified in the RBP Filing is a result solely of data center demand. 3

PJM’s approach will continue to impose data center costs on other customers. PJM fails to

correctly identify the source of the capacity market and reliability problem. PJM fails to

correctly identify the appropriate solution to the problem. As a result of the incorrect framing

of the problem, the details of the RBP Filing are largely irrelevant. The details are about

implementing a design that cannot achieve the correct objective of ensuring that data centers

bear their own costs. The significant issues with the design details further reveal the flaws

within PJM’s approach.

       PJM actually denies the fact that the shortfall faced by PJM is the result of data center

load. PJM states (September 10th Answer at 64): “It is fallacious to suggest that a just and

reasonable cost allocation approach must either identify specific loads (which are not FPA-

jurisdictional actors) and not the LSEs serving those loads or be limited to one type of load

when the resource adequacy shortfall is caused by all types of loads that comprise the subject

Load Adjustments” [emphasis in original].)

       The underlying theme and narrative of PJM’s RBP and IRAS Filings is that data center

load is just load and the normal PJM capacity market and energy market mechanisms can

handle the impact of data center load. PJM even goes a step beyond and incorrectly asserts

that the identified shortfall is a result of all types of loads. In a word, PJM asserts that it is just

supply and demand.4 PJM fails to recognize that the massive influx of data center load

requires a paradigm shift in thinking about capacity. PJM fails to recognize that the massive

influx of data centers requires a policy decision. That policy decision cannot reasonably fall

back on simple high school economic nostrums. The policy instruction from a wide range of

sources, including the elected representatives of the 67 million residents in PJM’s market area,




3    See Monitoring Analytics, LLC “Analysis of the 2027/2028 RPM Base Residual Auction – Part A,”
     (January 5, 2026).

4    See Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a
     Large Load Registry to Address System Reliability, Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (2026) (“IRAS Filing”).


                                                 -2-
 is clear. Data centers should pay for their own costs. A significant part of data center costs is

the cost of the capacity required to serve them. PJM’s proposals fail to conform to that policy

instruction.

       PJM attempts to use its current capacity cost allocation mechanism for the obligations

that result from the RBP with EDCs/LSEs at the center and in which EDCs/LSEs receive an

allocation of capacity costs from PJM and then allocate those costs to customers on a peak

load basis. The current cost allocation process is clearly not adequate to address the

assignment of data center costs to data centers. Rather than directly addressing the problem,

PJM’s proposal would push the issue to the states by suggesting that states can create

allocation rules that the EDCs/LSEs must follow.

       The September 10th Answer fails to address these underlying issues primarily by

ignoring the real policy issue and focusing on narrow technical issues of how to implement

the misguided RBP approach.

       On August 21, 2026, the Market Monitor submitted a protest demonstrating that the

RBP Filing has not been supported as just and reasonable. The Market Monitor’s protest also

demonstrated that the RBP Filing is unjust and unreasonable, and that attempting to

implement it will severely damage PJM markets, impose data center costs on other customers

as an intended consequence, create unintended consequences, and compound that damage

for a period of 15 years. The Market Monitor concluded that, for all these reasons, the RBP

Filing should be rejected.

       The RBP Filing and PJM’s September 10th Answer would continue to impose the costs

of data center development on other customers. The RBP Filing and PJM’s September 10th

Answer would continue to add to the $29.4 billion of capacity market costs that have resulted

from the inclusion of data centers and PJM’s inaction to date by leaving 20,539.7 MW of data




                                              -3-
 center load in the 2029/2030 BRA to be run in December 2026. 5 6 While appearing to recognize

that data center load is the source of the reliability issues facing PJM, PJM’s actual proposal

would impose the costs and risks of the proposed RBP solution on other customers. The

shortfall identified by PJM is entirely the result of existing and forecast data center load, yet

PJM has failed to verify the underlying details of the forecast and refuses to reduce the

forecast, and therefore the shortfall, based on known changes to data center plans. The costs

of addressing the shortfall within the RBP approach are inflated as a result of PJM’s failure

to include any market power mitigation rules, failure to use a single clearing price auction

and the creation of crushing collateral requirements for EDCs/LSEs and their customers.

       The September 10th Answer entirely fails to address the most fundamental issues

raised in the Market Monitor’s protest. The central error in the RBP Filing was not addressed

in the September 10th Answer. PJM assigns the responsibility for the identified shortfall to

individual EDCs that have data centers in their areas and to their customers despite the

irrefutable fact that the RBP shortfall is entirely the result of data center load. PJM’s approach

directly contradicts the principle that data center costs should be paid by data centers and

not by other customers. PJM does not explain why it is just and reasonable to assign the costs

of data center loads to EDCs/LSEs. PJM proposes to penalize EDCs and their customers for

the locational decisions of data centers. As a result of the fact that PJM is avoiding taking

responsibility for the final allocation of data center costs by EDCs, it is impossible to know

what the final outcome of PJM’s RBP Filing will be.

         PJM has the authority to require LSEs to condition wholesale service to data centers

on a requirement that data centers enter into bilateral contracts with generators that protect

other customers from the data center costs. 7

        Even if PJM were to allocate costs to other customers, PJM has the authority to allocate

the RBP costs to all PJM customers consistent with the allocation of backstop auction costs in

the current tariff. 8

        PJM asserts that it is not really allocating costs to the EDCs and their customers by

asserting that states can require the EDCs to allocate those costs to data centers. PJM is

attempting to evade its responsibility to directly ensure that data centers pay their own costs

by shifting that responsibility to the states and the EDCs. PJM denies responsibility for

allocating data center costs to data centers (at 56–58) by stating that this is not PJM’s job but

is the job of the states, based on an incorrect understanding of the FERC/PJM jurisdictional

authority. Despite all that, PJM does include a specific allocation of RBP data center costs to

LSEs (EDCs here) in the event that no alternative is created by individual states and

EDCs/LSEs are expected to allocate those costs to their customers per the method currently

used to allocate capacity costs. 9 10

        PJM focuses on the defined shortfall while ignoring the much larger issue of total

existing and forecast data center load. On a UCAP basis, the total data center load included

in the 2028/2029 BRA was 20,183.9 MW which is approximately three times the shortfall

identified by PJM. The September 10th Answer does not address this fundamental issue,

      2026) at 28–32.

 including the fact that data center load will continue to result in a significant increase in

capacity market costs for all customers in the upcoming 2029/2030 BRA in December 2026.

       The Market Monitor identified significant implementation issues in the RBP Filing

that the September 10th Answer fails to address. These issues, including the explicit failure to

address the exercise of market power, and the bafflingly complex implementation by PJM,

are all created by PJM’s misguided attempts to blame EDCs and their customers for the

addition of data center load rather than simply assigning the costs and risks of data center

load to data centers. For all these reasons, the RBP Filing is unjust and unreasonable and

should be rejected.

       The Market Monitor recognizes the urgency of the situation facing the PJM markets.

The Market Monitor continues to recommend that the Commission reject the RBP Filing and

direct PJM, under the Commission’s FPA Section 206 authority, to file, within two weeks, a

solution with the following elements:

       •   PJM should, working with LSEs and EDCs, immediately identify data center load

           not interconnected by June 1, 2026, and remove it from RPM capacity market

           auctions.

       •   PJM should establish criteria to be included in the RAA defining the obligations of

           LSEs to require that new data center loads have 15 year bilateral contracts with

           new generation that do not permit any cost or risk shifting to other customers. The

           contracts would be based on general terms and conditions in accordance with

           tariff defined criteria with the cost and risk specifics defined by the data centers

           and generators.

       •   For LSEs with data centers unable to make independent arrangements meeting the

           criteria, PJM should run a full single clearing price auction using the BRA capacity

           market clearing model for new data center load. LSEs would require data centers

           to participate in the reliability backstop auction if they do not have a bilateral

           contract for new generation that meets the requirements of such contracts. When

           the clearing process is complete, the LSEs would require that generators and data

                                              -6-
            center loads enter into 15 year bilateral contracts that do not permit any cost or

           risk shifting to other customers. The contracts would be based on general terms

           and conditions in accordance with tariff defined criteria with the cost and risk

           specifics defined by the data centers and generators.

       •   PJM should establish curtailment obligations for wholesale service to data centers

           during a defined transition period that would allow all data centers the time to

           contract for new generation.

       These requirements meet the goals of the Pledge and Principles and can be

implemented immediately.

I. ANSWER

       A. PJM’s Reliance on “Cooperative Federalism” Is Misguided and Has Resulted in
          a Flawed and Incomplete Proposal.

       The September 10th Answer defends (at 56–65) what it alleges is a “cost allocation

approach” in the RBP Filing with references to “cooperative federalism.” The RBP Filing does

not propose a cost allocation approach, it proposes to procure the 6,831.3 MW shortfall of

capacity through a flawed process that, by default, imposes the costs and risks of meeting

data center load on other customers. PJM hopes that the states will come up with additional

rules for allocating costs consistent with the broad consensus represented by the Pledge and




                                             -7-
 Principles. 11 12 PJM relies on speculation about what states may or may not do to complete its

proposal. The RBP Filing should be rejected as incomplete because it does not clearly state

how the costs and risks of meeting data center load must be assigned to customers. PJM failed

to file a complete regional solution consistent with its role as an RTO. PJM’s balkanized

approach is inefficient and ineffective at creating consistent regional markets. The

Commission has the jurisdiction needed to approve a complete proposal.

     Protection Pledge, leading United States hyperscalers and AI companies guarantee that data centers’

     “[p]rovide 15-year price certainty for new capacity resources” [emphasis]. The statement notes that
     this can be done in through a “Reliability Backstop Auction,” but does not require that this auction
     be a centralized procurement by PJM or that PJM customers assume risks. Second, “PJM should
     allocate the cost of any new capacity through the aforementioned Reliability Backstop Auction to
     load serving entities (LSEs) with new data centers that have not self-procured new capacity or agreed
     to be curtailable.” The principles, agreed to by the Governors of PJM States Indiana, Ohio, Maryland

     excluding risks of new resources or commitments to curtail. Additional principles that going beyond

     generator interconnections, i.e., the Reliability Resource Initiative (RRI), and (iv) continued efforts to
     reform the capacity market.

        PJM should ensure that the costs and risks of acquiring capacity to meet all data center

load, and not just the identified shortfall, are allocated to the data centers creating those costs

and risks in the PJM Region, consistent with the Pledge and Principles. Data centers and the

owners of new generation built to serve them are best positioned to understand and manage

the risks associated with building data centers and securing their power supply. It does not

serve the public interest to assign risk to customers who have no understanding and ability

to manage the associated risks. What states may or not do is unknown, but it cannot be

assumed the state regulators are better able to understand and manage these risks than data

centers and generators. The design flaws in the RBP Filing are required by PJM’s failure to

assign risks to those that create them.

       PJM reveals that it rejects the policy determination that underlies the Pledge and

Principles. 13 Although it attempts to hide behind an incorrect jurisdictional analysis, PJM

reveals here that it does not intend the RBP Filing to actually address the issue that it initially

identified as the reason for submitting the RBP Filing. 14 Failing to recognize the extraordinary

nature of data center demands treats existing customers unjustly and unreasonably. PJM

cannot show that its proposal is just and reasonable while failing to distinguish between new

data center load and existing load.

       PJM’s attempts to justify its incomplete RBP Filing based on an improper framing of

the Commission’s jurisdiction. States have jurisdiction over generation, and over retail sales

 in their own states. States do not have jurisdiction over neighboring states. PJM does not

show that states have the capability to perform the allocation consistent with the Pledge and

Principles. States cooperating with (or failing to cooperate with) other states to regulate

interstate commerce, displacing Federal regulation, is not cooperative federalism. PJM

should not attempt to transfer its responsibility to operate the regional capacity market to the

states. The Supreme Court has recognized that the Commission’s jurisdiction extends to rules

related to retail customers’ participation in the wholesale power markets as sellers. 15 The

Supreme Court recognizes Federal jurisdiction over the terms and conditions of retail

       PJM apparently believes that because data centers are retail customers, PJM cannot

require that the LSEs who serve them place terms and conditions on service to data centers.16

PJM has not reconciled this position with the jurisdiction exercised under the Reliability

Assurance Agreement (“RAA”). The RAA requires LSEs to meet their obligations from

capacity provided by generators that meet the terms and conditions of the RAA. 17 LSEs are

not permitted under the RAA to rely on Generation Capacity Resources that do not meet

 these terms and conditions regardless of state views about the capability of the facilities. 18

Resources included in Fixed Resource Requirement (“FRR”) Plans under Schedule 8.1 to the

RAA must also meet requirements specified in the RAA. 19

       PJM does not explain why it cannot propose terms and conditions related to data

centers through the LSEs that serve them when it can and does include terms and conditions

through LSEs (and other intermediate entities such as Curtailment Service Providers) on

other retail customers and on generation facilities. The reliability backstop procurement

would be a part of PJM’s rules designed to ensure resource adequacy through the capacity

markets and related rules. The capacity market rules are terms and conditions of wholesale

energy sales.

       The case for jurisdiction is stronger in this case than it was in EPSA. This case concerns

the procurement of capacity under proposed capacity market rules. The RBP Filing is a

modified version of the existing rules for reliability backstop auctions.20 The purpose of the

RBP is to address the particular and extraordinary demands related to resource adequacy

attributable to the rapid interconnection of data centers in the PJM Region. The Supreme

Court has recognized PJM and federal responsibility in this area to the point that such

responsibility preempts state action. 21 Data centers are receiving wholesale sales along with

the associated terms and conditions of such sales from PJM through Load Serving Entities.

        PJM allocates costs to EDCs based on the level of data center load in their areas that

the EDCs have provided to PJM through the large load adjustment process. 22 While PJM

asserts that it does not have jurisdiction over the allocation of costs to customers by the EDC,

the states do not develop allocation rules. 23 EDCs/LSEs are expected to allocate those costs to

their customers per the method currently used to allocate capacity costs. 24

       PJM denies responsibility for allocating data center costs to retail loads while making

critical decisions about that allocation. The RBP Filing would allocate the costs of meeting

data center load to EDCs rather than to data centers.

       PJM’s attempt to justify its incomplete proposal based on an incorrect jurisdictional

analysis and to instead rely on speculation about actions that states may take is insufficient

to support the RBP Filing as just and reasonable. PJM’s approach is unjust and unreasonable.

The RBP Filing should be rejected for that reason.

       B. The September 10th Answer Fails to Address the Issues Raised by the Market
          Monitor and Others.

               1. The Shortfall is Entirely the Result of Data Center Load.

       It is a matter of fact that the apparently very precise 6,831.3 MW of shortfall is the

result solely of data center load and that the shortfall MW are not correct.

               2. The Shortfall MW Value Is Not Correct and PJM Refuses to Correct It.

       It is a matter of fact that PJM’s MW shortfall target is not correct. PJM provided no

actual response to this point in the September 10th Answer other than to state that it is ok to

be incorrect. PJM plans to reduce the shortfall for opt out MW but refuses to reduce the

shortfall based on reductions in identified data center loads.

       The shortfall procurement target is based on the 2028/2029 BRA held in July 2026. PJM

set the procurement target to the deficit calculated as the difference between the RTO

reliability requirement and the total cleared MW in the 2028/2029 BRA. In the 2028/2029 BRA,

the deficit was 6,831.3 MW. The data center load forecast for the 2028/2029 BRA was based

data center projects have been cancelled. The Market Monitor calculated that 4,016.9 MW or

42 percent of the forecasted increase in the data center load between the 2026/2027 Delivery

Year and 2028/2029 Delivery Year have been cancelled or delayed as of September 21, 2026. 28

for 51 percent and the AEP-Ohio EDC accounted for 29 percent. There are no provisions in

the RBP Filing to revise the data center load forecast and the target procurement prior to the

RBP procurement process.

6,831.3 MW is “deliberately conservative” and “allowing procurement of capacity beyond

used the load forecast that included EDC provided large load adjustments, which were based

on inputs from data center developers (see Table 1). These estimates are understood to

include speculative load and have been significantly revised in the past and are likely to be

               5. PJM Ignores Fundamental Locational Market Requirements.

       The RBP Filing and September 10th Answer ignore the locational requirements that

are an essential part of the capacity market. The PJM Capacity Market has been, from the

genesis of the RPM design in 2007 based on locational reliability differences, been a locational

market. The PJM Capacity Market includes Locational Deliverability Areas (“LDA”). PJM

calculates a reliability requirement for every LDA with Capacity Emergency Transfer Limit

(“CETL”) that exceeds the LDA’s Capacity Emergency Transfer Objective (“CETO”) by 115

percent or meets other criteria. PJM has been using CETO and CETL metrics to account for

transmission network constraints that prevent capacity in one part of the system from reliably

serving load in another part of the PJM system. PJM’s failure to account for the actual location

of data centers and the generation to serve them will create additional and unnecessary costs

for all customers.

       The central objective of PJM’s Reliability Pricing Model is to limit potential loss of load

events to approximately one event every 10 years at the RTO level. PJM applies a stricter

criterion to ensure that the transmission constraints do not reduce reliability. PJM’s standard

is approximately one event every 25 years for every modeled LDA.

incorrectly calculated and static capacity only payment creates significant risk for generators

and for customers by failing to account for energy market net revenues during the contract

term.

         PJM’s RBP Filing fails to account for the likely scenario in which data center load

increases energy prices and increases net revenues yet customers have to pay the RBP price

that does not reflect the increased revenues to generators.

         These critical elements of the RBP design are not consistent with the design of the

current backstop auction. The current backstop auction rules are based on the actual net costs

of generators and reflect actual net revenues over the 15 year life of the contracts. 71 The

current rules provide for payment of 100 percent of the required revenue, accounting for both

energy and capacity revenues. PJM fails to provide a reason for deviating from the current

design.

                 7. PJM’s Definitions of Capacity That Can Satisfy the Requirements to
                    Meet Data Center Load are Inconsistent.

         In the IMM Protest at 19-22, the Market Monitor explained the differences in PJM’s

definitions of the qualifying criteria for RBP resources and the RBP offset. In PJM’s September

10th Answer, PJM fails to address any of the concerns raised by the Market Monitor. The

problem is that PJM proposes to treat RBP offset capacity as equivalent to RBP supply for

 purposes of reducing the regional reliability requirement, even though the two have

materially different contractual protections and performance obligations.

       In the September 10th Answer at 29, PJM states, “To be clear, the eligibility

requirements for Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP and RBP Resources are not the same.” PJM

states that both the RBP resources and the RBP offset would contribute to addressing the

resource adequacy shortfall. But that contribution is not the same. In the September 10th

Answer at 32, PJM claims that comparing the RBP resource and RBP offset requirements is

an erroneous comparison. However, PJM is proposing to treat them as equivalent for

reducing the procurement target. The comparison is relevant because the RBP Filing treats

them as substitutes.

       In the September 10th Answer at 33-34, PJM argues that the less stringent requirements

for the RBP offset are meant to encourage parties to voluntarily enter into bilateral

arrangements rather than reliance on the RBP framework. PJM is choosing the preferred

approach to be bilateral contracts in defining their proposal. In the RBP Filing (at 40), PJM

states that “bilateral agreements may not need to be longer than five years to develop new

capacity [Italics added].” PJM does not provide any substantive support for the less stringent

5 year term of the RBP offset or for the differing criteria for RBP resources and the RBP offset.

PJM does not explain how this contributes to reliability or to price stability over the next 15

years or how it interacts with the other elements of the RBP Filing.

       In addition, the RBP Filing and IRAS Filing have inconsistent definitions of capacity

that can be used to satisfy the requirements to meet the data center load. The IRAS Filing

allows 10 year contracts for Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) that could terminate

after three years, whereas the RBP auction would require 15 year contracts but would also

allow a five year bilateral contract to meet the same obligation under the RBP offset option.

       The RBP Filing includes inconsistent definitions of capacity that will result in

unintended consequences for reliability and capacity market prices in the future. One result

of the weaker requirements will be that data center load is returned to the capacity market

sooner and will impose additional costs on other customers sooner. While this may be PJM’s

 own costs rather than imposing their costs on other customers.
